title: Good Seeing
subtitle: A summit observatory above the clouds, the night the owner drives his investors up
story:
The old observatory on the volcano's summit has one worker left: you. The island's new owner is building his resort far below, and tonight he is driving its investors up to look through the telescope. If they like what they see, the observatory stays open. If not, it closes. He has his pitch ready: "The astronomer spent decades sorting galaxies by eye. On his last season's plates, call everything a spiral and you're right 9 times in 10, so why pay an astronomer?"

Before their headlights reach the summit, open the astronomer's photographic plates: the training plates he classified for the main catalogue, and the held-back plates of his last season, kept in a notebook he never merged. Fit a model that gives each galaxy a probability of being an elliptical, predict the held-back plates at the 0.5 cut-off, and find which predictor drives it. Then score its accuracy against calling everything a spiral, and count the ellipticals it caught. Show what his rule misses, then open the dome.

escapeBrief: Good Seeing. The player is the last worker at an old observatory on the volcano's summit, above the cloud sea, while the resort is being built far below. The villain, keen to stop paying for the place, is driving the resort's investors up tonight to look through the telescope: if they see something truly spectacular, the observatory stays open; if not, it closes. The rooms are a chain joined only by separate segments of outside deck. The sky above the deck is clear all the way; below it the cloud sea breaks up along the chain, until the last segment shows the road and their headlights climbing it. Each segment carries one sky instrument, read in passing: the moon dial (moonlight washes out faint fuzzy things), the twinkle scope (bad seeing blurs planets and close doubles), the glow meter (the resort's floodlights brighten that side of the sky and hurt anything low there), and the star-count board (how dark and clear it is). Tonight: moon 8, twinkle 8, glow 8, stars 11 of 20. The graded puzzles are the door locks; the boss opens the dome. ESCAPE. The old astronomer's showpiece bank holds twelve cards, one per VIP showpiece, each engraved with its dome bearing and telescope altitude for tonight. Four shafts run along it, one per sky instrument, and each card takes each shaft through its own gear (or a bare pin where that reading does not matter to it), so one setting moves all twelve differently; each card's bead rides an S-shaped slot to a probability, against one shared red cut-off. The villain's brochure promises the crowd-pleasers (Saturn's rings, the Great Nebula, Andromeda, the Seven Sisters, the comet), and on an ordinary night they pass. Tonight the moon washes out Andromeda, the twinkle blurs Saturn's rings, the moon and his own floodlights together kill the comet and the Great Nebula low over the resort, and the moon, helped by the floodlights, dims the Seven Sisters above it. Set tonight's readings and exactly one card lights: the Gold & Blue Pair, a bright, wide double star that none of it touches. Key its bearing and altitude, 29323, on the pointing console in the dome. The dome is slow: three pointings, then their headlights reach the summit (a bend closer per pointing, seen through the dome's east port). Each miss shows that object's poor view through the eyepiece (or empty sky). After the third miss they arrive, look, and drive off, and the observatory closes; reload to try again. Unguessability: twelve cards and three tries, and the brochure picks all fail; the code is read off the right card. Echo: predict a whole table at once against a cut-off, and the same input matters differently for each case. Ending: the dome slews, the investors look, and the observatory stays open.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: This scenario was logistic regression for classification: a probability from several predictors, a cut-off, and a held-back set where you counted what the model caught and missed. A rule that is right most of the time can still catch none of the cases that matter. Here is what you did.

done.title: The view is ready
done.body: His pitch rested on accuracy, and on the held-back plates the model is barely behind him. But calling everything a spiral catches none of the ellipticals; the model catches thirteen. The dome is open. Down the mountain, the investors' headlights are climbing the last bends. You have three pointings before they arrive. Show them something worth keeping the observatory open for.

escapeDone.title: Good seeing
escapeDone.body: The telescope swings west and settles. In the eyepiece, a gold star and a blue one hang side by side, sharp and still, while everything the brochure promised drowns in moonlight and glare. The investors take turns at the eyepiece and stop talking about the resort. By morning the observatory has its funding for another year.

rooms.designNote:
ARRIVAL (rooms[0]). Racks of glass plates in sleeves and the 1948 catalogue; the villain's brochure and pitch letter on the bench (tonight's arrangements, moved here from the office at 4b under Lucas's clue waiver). A front door from the road path is the way in (scenery, not a hotspot). The deck door is a heavy storm door dogged by a brass hand-wheel: the wheel is the rung 1 gate. training_plates <- galaxy_plates %>% filter(record == "training")
held_back_plates <- galaxy_plates %>% filter(record == "held back")
PROMPT: Fit a model that predicts `elliptical` from `color_index` on the training plates. What probability does it give the galaxy G-1948-5198? Store it, to two decimal places, in `answer`.
CODE: color_model <- buildModel(data = training_plates, model_type = "logistic_regression", predictors = "color_index", response = "elliptical"); predictWithModel(data = training_plates, model = color_model) %>% filter(galaxy == "G-1948-5198") %>% select(galaxy, color_index, probability_yes); answer <- 0.71
ANSWER 0.7078 (color_index 0.98), abs(answer - 0.7078) <= 0.01. Intercept -21.70, slope 23.05.
REJECTED readings (outside the tolerance): forgetting the training filter 0.601; all five predictors 0.763; base rate 0.045; 0.5; elliptical rate among the 5/10/20/30/50/100 nearest training galaxies by colour 0.40/0.60/0.60/0.633/0.54/0.35; galaxies with the same reading 1.000; at or above it 0.667.
FORM check (a number for a named galaxy). The color_index units are the trap by design: it is the weak predictor that looks strongest on one-at-a-time correlation (rung 3).

rooms.technique: model accuracy versus a base-rate rule
rooms.designNote:
Catalogue ledgers on the desk and the switchboard that runs the dome (the brochure and pitch letter moved to the plate vault at 4b). The boss gate is the dome (one gate, counted once), not the doors here: both are ungated, so deck_stars and its board are reachable before the boss (harmless). BOSS (check; opens the dome via the office knife switch). PROMPT: He says calling every galaxy a spiral is right 9 times in 10. On the held-back plates, score the accuracy of your model at the 0.5 cut-off and of calling everything a spiral: which is right on more galaxies? Now count what matters: of the held-back galaxies that are ellipticals, how many did your model catch? Store that number of galaxies in `answer`.
CODE: plate_predictions %>% summarize(model_right = sum(predicted_class == elliptical), always_no_right = sum(elliptical == "no")); plate_predictions %>% filter(elliptical == "yes", predicted_class == "yes") %>% summarize(n = n()); answer <- 13
ANSWER 13. "Call everything a spiral" is right on 270 of 300 (90.0%), the model on 265 (88.3%); the model says yes on 31: 13 caught, 18 false alarms (precision 42%), 17 missed; the rule catches 0.
Tempting readings, none 13: 31, 30, 18, 17, 265, 270, 88, 90, 300. Use summarize(n = n()), not count() (masked by seqinr).
Gate: solving it frees the office knife switch (dial dome_power), which opens deck_stars -> dome.

rooms.debrief: A rule that is right on most galaxies can still catch none of the ones that matter. On the held-back plates, calling every galaxy a spiral was right on 270 of 300 and the model on 265, yet the model caught 13 of the 30 ellipticals and the rule caught none. Accuracy and the number of cases caught measure different things, and here they disagree; the number caught, with the false alarms beside it, is the evidence for whether the model does the job.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you fit a model with one predictor, color index, on the training plates and read the probability it gave one named galaxy, about 0.71.

In the second puzzle you fit a model on all five predictors, predicted the held-back plates and picked the galaxy rated most likely to be an elliptical, which stood well clear of the rest at about 0.99.

In the third puzzle you scaled the five predictors, refit the model and compared the size of their coefficients, and concentration drove the probability most, where the unscaled coefficients had pointed to color index.

In the final puzzle you scored the model against calling every galaxy a spiral on the held-back plates: the rule was right on more galaxies, 270 of 300 against 265, yet it caught none of the 30 ellipticals and the model caught 13.
To escape you set the night's four sky readings on the showpiece bank, found the one card that cleared the cut-off, and keyed its bearing and altitude on the pointing console.
